front_blocks.md: Define **atom**.

back_blocks.md: An **atom** is the smallest particle of an element, containing **electrons** surrounding a **nucleus** that holds **protons** and **neutrons**.

cards.back_md: An **atom** is the smallest particle of an element, containing **electrons** surrounding a **nucleus** that holds **protons** and **neutrons**.

front_blocks.md: Define **molecule**.

back_blocks.md: A **molecule** is a group of two or more **atoms** chemically combined to form an identifiable unit that retains the properties and composition of the substance.

cards.back_md: A **molecule** is a group of two or more **atoms** chemically combined to form an identifiable unit that retains the properties and composition of the substance.

front_blocks.md: Where are protons and neutrons found in an atom?

back_blocks.md: Protons and neutrons are found in the **nucleus**, at the centre of the atom. The nucleus is **positively charged**.

cards.front_md: Where are protons and neutrons found in an atom?
cards.back_md: Protons and neutrons are found in the **nucleus**, at the centre of the atom. The nucleus is **positively charged**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Electrons have a relative mass of 1, the same as protons.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Electrons have a **negligible** relative mass (approximately 1/1840 of a proton). Only **protons** and **neutrons** have a relative mass of 1.

front_blocks.md: The three subatomic particles that make up an atom are **..........**, **..........** and **..........**.

back_blocks.md: The three subatomic particles that make up an atom are **protons**, **neutrons** and **electrons**.

cards.front_md: The three subatomic particles that make up an atom are **..........**, **..........** and **..........**.

front_blocks.md: What is the **atomic number** of an element?

back_blocks.md: **Atomic number** is the number of **protons** in the nucleus of an atom. In a neutral atom, it also equals the number of **electrons**.

cards.front_md: What is the **atomic number** of an element?
cards.back_md: **Atomic number** is the number of **protons** in the nucleus of an atom. In a neutral atom, it also equals the number of **electrons**.

front_blocks.md: How do you calculate the number of neutrons in an atom?

back_blocks.md: The number of **neutrons** is calculated by subtracting the **atomic number** from the **mass number**: neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

cards.front_md: How do you calculate the number of neutrons in an atom?

front_blocks.md: What is the **mass number** of an atom?

back_blocks.md: **Mass number** is the total number of **protons** and **neutrons** in the nucleus of an atom.

cards.front_md: What is the **mass number** of an atom?
cards.back_md: **Mass number** is the total number of **protons** and **neutrons** in the nucleus of an atom.

front_blocks.md: Define **isotope**.

back_blocks.md: An **isotope** is one of two or more atoms of the same element that have the same number of **protons** but a different number of **neutrons**.

cards.back_md: An **isotope** is one of two or more atoms of the same element that have the same number of **protons** but a different number of **neutrons**.

front_blocks.md: What is **relative atomic mass** (*A*<sub>r</sub>)?

back_blocks.md: **Relative atomic mass** (*A*<sub>r</sub>) is the average mass of one atom of an element, taking into account the **abundance** of all its **isotopes**. It is relative to 1/12 the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

cards.back_md: **Relative atomic mass** (*A*<sub>r</sub>) is the average mass of one atom of an element, taking into account the **abundance** of all its **isotopes**. It is relative to 1/12 the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

front_blocks.md: Why is the relative atomic mass of an element often not a whole number?

back_blocks.md: The **relative atomic mass** is an average that accounts for all the **isotopes** of an element and their **relative abundances**. If an element has isotopes with different masses, the average may fall between whole numbers.

cards.front_md: Why is the relative atomic mass of an element often not a whole number?
cards.back_md: The **relative atomic mass** is an average that accounts for all the **isotopes** of an element and their **relative abundances**. If an element has isotopes with different masses, the average may fall between whole numbers.

front_blocks.md: To calculate *A*<sub>r</sub>, multiply the mass of each **..........** by its percentage **..........**, add the results together, then divide by **..........**.

back_blocks.md: To calculate *A*<sub>r</sub>, multiply the mass of each **isotope** by its percentage **abundance**, add the results together, then divide by **100**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Isotopes of the same element have different numbers of protons.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same **atomic number** (same proton count) but different **mass numbers** (different numbers of neutrons).

front_blocks.md: A sample of rubidium contains 72% <sup>85</sup>Rb and 28% <sup>87</sup>Rb. What is the relative atomic mass of this sample?

back_blocks.md: The **relative atomic mass** is calculated as:

cards.front_md: A sample of rubidium contains 72% <sup>85</sup>Rb and 28% <sup>87</sup>Rb. What is the relative atomic mass of this sample?
cards.back_md:
The **relative atomic mass** is calculated as:

*A*<sub>r</sub> = [(72 × 85) + (28 × 87)] ÷ 100 = (6120 + 2436) ÷ 100 = **85.6**

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The relative atomic mass of an element can be calculated using only one isotope.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
The relative atomic mass must account for **all isotopes** and their **percentage abundances**. Using only one isotope would give just the mass of that isotope, not a true average.

front_blocks.md: How do you recognise isotopes from their nuclear notation?

back_blocks.md: You can recognise isotopes by looking at their notation: they share the same chemical **symbol** but carry different **mass numbers** as superscripts. For example, <sup>63</sup>Cu and <sup>65</sup>Cu are both isotopes of copper.
